summary: Gobbler's Knob is a restored 1933 NPS rustic-style two-story lookout in Mount Rainier National Park, staffed into the 1980s and now used as a hiking destination and standby ranger lookout.

facts.design: Two-story NPS rustic-style frame structure, about 14x14 feet, live-in cab with catwalk on the upper level, storage below, secured with cables to buried deadmen

staffing.status: no longer staffed full-time for fire detection; used as standby site by backcountry rangers

access.note: Within Mount Rainier National Park; reached by hiking trail, popular hiking destination.

events.note: Two-story frame lookout built, designed by the NPS Branch of Plans and Design under acting chief architect Edwin A. Nickel.
Staffed into the 1980s as an active fire lookout (decade-level precision only).
Added to the National Register of Historic Places, March 13, 1991; part of the Mount Rainier National Historic Landmark District.
Registered on the National Historic Lookout Register, March 31, 2003 (per queue brief, from NHLR detail page).
Extensively damaged in a windstorm, along with Mount Fremont Fire Lookout; both were later repaired/restored.

evidence.supports: Closest of the park's four lookouts to the peak; two-story NPS design, 14x14 cab with catwalk, restored, used by backcountry rangers as standby site
evidence.quote: Gobblers Knob Lookout to the southwest of Mt. Rainier is the closest to the peak of the four lookouts in the National Park and a popular hiking destination. Built in 1933, the two story frame NPS design structure with 14'x14' live-in cab with catwalk has been restored and is also used by backcountry rangers as a standby detection site.

evidence.supports: Built 1933, designed by NPS Branch of Plans and Design under Edwin A. Nickel, two-story with balconied lookout and storage below, cables to deadmen, NRHP listing 1991, 2006 storm damage and repair
evidence.quote: The building is about 14 feet (4.3 m) by 14 feet (4.3 m), and was designed by the National Park Service Branch of Plans and designs under the supervision of Acting Chief Architect Edwin A. Nickel. It was built in 1933. The two-story structure features a balconied lookout on the second level, with storage on the ground level. Cables secured to deadmen keep the lookout from blowing over... The lookout was extensively damaged in a 2006 storm, along with Mount Fremont Fire Lookout, with both since being repaired.

evidence.supports: NRHP listing date and Historic Landmark District
evidence.quote: Added to NRHP March 13, 1991... It is part of the Mount Rainier National Historic Landmark District, which encompasses the entire park
Built in 1933, this 2-story frame cab was staffed into the 1980's.
